$comment:
REQ-TWN-001/002/003 and v1.0 §9. Every number the town reads lives here — the grid it is built on, the per-capita demand that turns a population into pressure, and the weights that summarise that pressure as Town Stability. Nothing in systems/town/ carries a constant.

The one value worth defending: `stability.weights` deliberately does not sum to 1. Stability is a summary of three independent pressures, and normalising it would let a catastrophic housing failure be averaged away by a full granary. See DL-036.

grid.$comment: Small enough that a Small Camp looks sparse and a Hunter City looks full. Build mode is a toggle over this grid with four-direction rotation (v1.0 §9).

population.$comment: REQ-TWN-003. Population creates demand; buildings create capacity; the mismatch is pressure. Growth is driven by reputation and prosperity, and it stalls — never reverses into a death spiral — when the town cannot support anyone else.

perCapita.$comment: A bed and a meal each; services are shared, so one service point covers about four people. At 1.0 the starting town could not service its own starting population and immediately began losing residents — a new guild opening on a crisis it had no means to fix.

growth.$comment: Arrivals per coarse step. `perReputation` is arrivals per point of reputation; `prosperityScale` multiplies by how comfortably the town is already coping, so a strained town attracts nobody.

departure.$comment: Sustained pressure loses people. Deliberately slower than growth: a bad month should cost the player something without unwinding an hour of building.

stability.$comment: REQ-TWN-003: Town Stability summarises but never replaces the individual food, housing and service indicators. Weights are relative severities, not shares.

recovery.$comment:
Repays the Phase 3 placeholder. v1.0 §4 requires recovery to vary measurably with time, food, housing and service quality, so the base rate here is what a baseline town achieves and every town term multiplies it (core/hunter/availability.recoveryRatePerStep).

`injuryStepsAtBaseline` is the length of an injury in a town with exactly baseline housing, food and services — a better town shortens it, a strained one lengthens it. The old flat INJURY_TICKS/RECOVERY_TICKS constants are gone.
recovery.$cadenceNote: The fine-ticks-per-coarse-step figure used to live here too, and had already drifted from the clock it was meant to mirror. DL-020 makes that cadence a property of the simulation clock; everything that needs it now asks the clock.

quality.$comment: A town with no housing at all is not a town with baseline housing — these are the floors used when nothing has been built, so an unbuilt town recovers badly rather than normally. Capacity ratios above 1 raise quality with diminishing returns rather than linearly, or overbuilding would trivialise recovery.

stages.$comment: REQ-TWN-002 — Small Camp -> Village -> Fortified Town -> Hunter City, with no reset on progression. Requirements are minimums that must all hold; the stage reached is the highest satisfied, and Town records the highest ever reached so a stage is never lost (DL-037).

reputation.$comment: Makes REQ-WLD-002's reputation unlock axis evaluable — it was parsed and reported as 'not yet tracked' through Phase 5. Earned by doing the work the frontier notices: clearing routes, killing wardens, coming home. Bounded so it cannot be farmed into meaninglessness on blue zones.

assignment.$comment: REQ-TWN-009/010 and DL-008. Preferred role and preferred department are scoring INPUTS. They are weights here, next to the capability terms they compete with, precisely so nobody can reintroduce them as vetoes — a preference that can be outweighed is structurally not a veto.
assignment.$note: attributeFit (0.5) strictly outweighs both preferences combined (0.35), so a well-suited hunter is assigned over a badly-suited one who asked for the job. That ordering is the whole content of DL-008, and it is not left to good intentions: parseDepartments rejects any department policy preset whose modified preference weights would reach attributeFit, and tests/town.test.ts sweeps every preset to prove a hopeless volunteer still loses to a capable draftee.
assignment.$note2: `capability` is a separate weight from `attributeFit`, and that separation is load-bearing rather than tidy. They were one multiplied term at first — alignment times development — and because both factors sit below 1, the combined term could only reach about a third of its weight at realistic levels, which let a flat 0.22 preference beat it outright. DL-008 was violated in play while the load-time guard, comparing configured weights, reported everything correct. A guard over weights is only sound if each term can actually reach its weight.
assignment.$note3: `outputValue` is the AI's own optimisation (v1.0 §2.1 rank 3): between two jobs a hunter is equally suited to, it prefers the one that produces more. Without it the rota was purely a suitability match, so a guild whose hunters were all best at drilling put its whole roster in the drill yard and never staffed the hunting camp — the posts existed and were unreachable. It sits below attributeFit deliberately: the AI may prefer more valuable work, it may not override who is actually good at it.

departments.$comment: REQ-DEP-001/002/004. There is deliberately no budget field of any kind (REQ-DEP-003 / conflict A10, enforced by tests/architecture.test.ts). A department is staff, a head and a policy — never an allowance.

headQualification.$comment: How much a qualified head is worth. A department with no head falls back to a deputy (the best-scoring member) at reduced effect, and to the Guild AI at the floor — never to zero, because a leaderless department should underperform rather than stop.

performance.$comment: Multi-metric by design (REQ-DEP-004): one number per department would hide exactly the trade-off the player is making. `staffingTarget` is heads-per-department at which staffing reads as fully met.

priorities.$comment: Player-set priority per department, and the default spread. Guild policy remains the highest authority (REQ-DEP-004) — priority is a weight in the assignment score, not an override of it.
